claims.text: The identity of X governs protective oxide formation in CrFeCoNiX alloys above 900 °C.
Al has a strong oxygen affinity that promotes rapid formation of a continuous Al2O3-rich scale.
The Al2O3-rich scale on CrFeCoNiAl is slow-growing, stable, and coherent with the substrate.
CrFeCoNiMn and CrFeCoNiSi form mixed or less-adherent oxides that tend to crack or spall.
Higher oxide-growth stress and thermal-expansion mismatch cause cracking or spallation in the Mn- and Si-containing alloys.
The alloying element drives surface enrichment and determines the oxide phases that form.
A dense, adherent Al2O3 layer mediates oxidation protection in CrFeCoNiAl.
Mn or Si produces mixed or less-coherent oxides exhibiting microcracking.
Al has a lower diffusion rate in the alloy matrix.
Al forms a slow-growing, low-expansion Al2O3 layer that bonds well to the substrate.
Mn and Si form complex multiphase oxides with larger volumetric changes.
The larger volumetric changes of Mn- and Si-associated oxides generate internal stresses that cause cracking and eventual spallation.
Under identical high-temperature exposure, CrFeCoNiAl will retain a more uniform, coherent, and adherent protective scale than CrFeCoNiMn or CrFeCoNiSi.
CrFeCoNiMn and CrFeCoNiSi will exhibit greater weight gain and substrate degradation than CrFeCoNiAl.
Comparable microstructure and identical thermal and atmospheric exposure allow X = Al to be tested against X = Mn and X = Si as controlled baselines.
Failure of CrFeCoNiAl to show statistically significant improvements in weight gain, cracking or spallation, and adhesion relative to both comparison alloys would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The intervention and boundary specify temperatures above 900 °C, whereas the conditions include 900–950 °C, which permits exposure at exactly 900 °C.
